source: Glucksberg (1964) Functional fixedness: problem solution as a function of observing responses
finding: Duncker's candle problem run in touch-only form with 10 blindfolded students. Solution times compared with Glucksberg (1962) sighted groups. A box full of tacks (container function shown) is solved far slower and fails more often than an empty box.
numbers: Sighted, box full of tacks (Dm-): N=32, mean 11.08 min (SD 4.84), 16 of 32 failed at the 15 min cap. Sighted, empty box (Dm+): N=32, mean 3.67 min (SD 4.52), 2 of 32 failed. Touch form, full box: N=10, mean 5.47 min (SD 5.13), 2 failed. Money prize of $10 for fastest.
limits: Small N in the touch group. The comparison groups come from an earlier study, not randomised together. 1960s adults, one object.
agent_relevance: Cleanest size of the classic effect: showing an object in its usual role roughly triples time and doubles failure. Maps to a prompt that has already framed an item by its usual use.

source: Glucksberg (1964) Functional fixedness: problem solution as a function of observing responses
finding: Solution never happened on the first touch of the fixed object. Of the 8 solvers, 7 solved on an accidental later contact with the box (adventitious); 1 on an exploratory contact. The author reads this as the cue (box) meeting the problem formulation by contiguity, not as a plan that then searches for an object.
numbers: 10 male undergraduates. Box contacts before solution ranged from 5 to 17. Two subjects hit the 15 min cap. Solution time 0.60 to 7.02 min among solvers.
limits: Author says the contiguity account is compatible with the data, not directly proven. Tiny sample.
agent_relevance: Suggests a new use arrives when the object and the goal are active together. Hints that putting the goal and a list of parts in the same context step may matter more than asking the model to 'think of new uses'.

source: Fleck and Weisberg (2004) The use of verbal protocols as data: an analysis of insight in the candle problem
finding: 58 Temple undergraduates did Duncker's candle problem silent or thinking aloud. Talking aloud did not change the box-solution rate. Only about a quarter solve it in the standard filled-box form.
numbers: Box solution: 8 of the thinking-aloud group (23.5%) vs 5 of the silent group (27.7%); chi-square(1,N=52)=0.113, p=.736. Overall 25% (n=13), mean solve time 5.72 min (SD 3.13). Matches 25% reported by Weisberg and Suls (1973) and Glucksberg and Weisberg (1966). 10 min limit.
limits: Verbal overshadowing (Schooler et al. 1993) was not replicated here; authors note that effect may be unstable.
agent_relevance: Base rate for the founding task: about 1 in 4 breaks the fixation in 10 min. Also: writing out reasoning did not hurt solution here, so a written trace does not by itself cause fixation.

source: Fleck and Weisberg (2004) The use of verbal protocols as data: an analysis of insight in the candle problem
finding: What people try first in the candle problem, coded from protocols. Three quarters start from the tacks, only a few from the box. The container use of the box is the dominant first frame.
numbers: First solution built around: tacks about 75%, wax of the candle 14%, matches or matchbook 6%, box 4%.
limits: One lab sample, one problem.
agent_relevance: Shows what 'the dominant first frame' looks like in data. A scaffold could count how many attempts share one frame before allowing a re-description step.

source: Fleck and Weisberg (2004) The use of verbal protocols as data: an analysis of insight in the candle problem
finding: Tests the impasse and restructuring account of insight (Ohlsson 1992; representational change). Restructuring was common. Impasse was not required, and having an impasse did not go with solving: those who never hit an impasse solved more often.
numbers: 44% showed some impasse. Box solution: 7 of 19 without impasse (37%) vs 1 of 15 with impasse (7%); 0 of 3 with true impasse. Of 213 failures, 128 (60%) were followed by impasse or restructuring.
limits: 10 min limit may be too short for impasse to resolve (authors). Coding of impasse is subjective. 34 protocols analysed.
agent_relevance: Evidence against a rule 'wait for a stall, then reframe'. Fits G1 only partly: the trigger for reframing in humans is failure, not a measured stall.

source: German and Defeyter (2000) Immunity to functional fixedness in young children
finding: Box task analogous to the candle problem with 60 children aged 5, 6 and 7. Showing the usual function (box as container of objects) slowed 6 and 7 year olds but not 5 year olds. Younger children were not fixated.
numbers: N=10 per cell. Percent giving box-as-support solution, preutilised vs not: age 5 60% vs 80%; age 6 60% vs 90%; age 7 40% vs 89% (Fisher p=.04 at age 7 only). Mean time (s): age 5 44.5 vs 55.8; age 6 113.8 vs 50.7; age 7 115.3 vs 28.9. Mann-Whitney age 6 U=2 p<.005, age 7 U=1 p<.01, age 5 n.s.
limits: Ten children per cell. Task is a toy analogue, not Duncker's own. Time analysis only on solvers.
agent_relevance: Fixation is learned: it grows with knowledge of the standard function. A more knowledgeable model is, by this logic, more exposed. Supports testing fixation by strength of prior.

source: German and Defeyter (2000) Immunity to functional fixedness in young children
finding: Sets out two mechanisms for why people stay stuck: the right plan is not retrieved (Keane), or the problem is encoded in a way that blocks it and must be restructured (Ohlsson 1984). They favour a developmental story: older children hold a tighter notion of what counts as an object's function. Cites German and Johnson: adults judge the original function as true function 86% of the time, 5 year olds 61%.
numbers: Adult 86% vs 5 year old 61% of choosing intended function (cited, not run here).
limits: Cited figures from other studies; interpretation is theirs.
agent_relevance: Two different repairs follow: widen retrieval (more diverse cues) or re-encode the problem (restate in generic terms). A scaffold needs both and a check on which one failed.

source: Marsh, Landau and Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity
finding: Replicates the conformity effect of Smith, Ward and Schumacher (1993): more examples shown, more copying of the examples' key features, in the alien-creature drawing task. But total output and elaborateness did not fall.
numbers: Exp 1: 80 students, 16 per group, five groups from 0 to 9 examples, 25 min drawing. Conformity (share of antennae, four legs, tail) rose with number of examples: omnibus F(4,75)=5.91, p<.01; linear F(1,75)=4.75. Critical features were 4.4% of all features in controls and 12.1% in the nine-example group. Number of creatures F<1; features per creature F(4,75)=1.40, p>.10.
limits: Authors question whether conformity equals a creativity constraint; only the proportion of copied features moved. Single task, undergraduates.
agent_relevance: Dose-response: copying rises with number of examples shown. Directly testable in prompts: vary shots 0,1,3,6,9 and count copied features.

source: Marsh, Landau and Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity
finding: Exp 2: examples that carried an artificial feature pair (antennae with claws) that never go together in real animals were copied more than controls, and those designs were rated more creative by independent raters. So copying a feature set is not always a loss in rated creativity.
numbers: About 77 students (df 2,74): artificial vs control contrast on the critical feature t(72)=3.2, p<.01; both critical features together appeared only in the artificial group. Independent creativity rating of artificial examples 3.29 vs natural 3.21 (SEM .16, .24). Number of creatures and complexity not different (F<1; F(2,74)=1.66).
limits: Rating of creativity by a second group; the metric of creativity is itself debated.
agent_relevance: Warns against measuring fixation only as 'copied the example'. The agent needs a measure of what was lost, not only what was copied.

source: Marsh, Landau and Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity
finding: Exp 3: a one day delay between seeing the examples and designing raised conformity, as models of unconscious plagiarism predict. Told not to copy, people still copied. Output counts and feature counts did not change.
numbers: 74 students, 36 immediate and 38 delayed, 3 examples shown 90 s. Conformity higher after delay: F(1,73)=4.74, p<.05; share of all features that were critical: F(1,73)=5.74, p<.05. Number of creatures F<1; mean features F<1. Novel, uncommon, miscellaneous feature classes fell by small, non-significant amounts (all F<2.5).
limits: Explanations compared (activation, retrieval blocking, category abstraction) are not cleanly separated by the data.
agent_relevance: Copying persists or grows with time and is a source-monitoring failure, not intent. In a long run, early outputs in context may leak into later ones without being seen as copies. Check late attempts against early ones by code.

source: Marsh, Landau and Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity
finding: Lays out the rival accounts of why examples are copied: (1) activated features accrue strength (activation); (2) activated exemplars block retrieval of others (Smith); (3) structured imagination, starting from a known category; (4) category abstraction: people infer a 'space creature' category from the examples and judge their own design against it. Source monitoring failure (cryptomnesia) explains why 'do not copy' fails.
limits: Authors say the data do not decide among accounts.
agent_relevance: Different accounts give different fixes. If category abstraction, a counter-example set helps; if blocking, a break and a changed cue helps; if source monitoring, tagging provenance by code helps.

source: Smith, Ward and Schumacher (1993) Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task
finding: Founding example-conformity study. Three experiments: people who saw three example creatures or toys copied the examples' critical features more than controls. Telling them to diverge as much as possible did not reduce copying (Exp 3). Number of creatures did not drop. Read here only through the descriptions in Marsh et al. 1996 and Vasconcelos and Crilly 2016.
numbers: Critical features of examples: four legs, a tail, antennae. Examples: 3 shown. Exact percentages not read in this session.
limits: Paper itself not opened (paywalled). Figures above are as described by citing papers.
agent_relevance: Source of the 'told to avoid, still copied' result that schema question (b) tests in LLMs.

source: Ward (1994) Structured imagination: the role of category structure in exemplar generation
finding: Founding structured-imagination paper. People asked to draw creatures on a distant planet gave creatures with Earth-animal properties: bilateral symmetry, sense organs, appendages. Under a lava planet constraint they added wings rather than non-animal parts. Asking for 'wildest imagination' did not remove the pattern (Exp 4). Read here only through descriptions in Marsh et al. 1996 and Ward et al. 2002.
numbers: Four experiments (as described). Per-condition figures not read in this session.
limits: Paper itself not opened (paywalled).
agent_relevance: Core claim for our scaffold: new ideas start from the most accessible category member and copy its defaults. Defaults can be listed by code, then forbidden.

source: Ward, Patterson, Sifonis, Dodds and Saunders (2002) The role of graded category structure in imaginative thought
finding: Tests why people start from particular Earth animals. Items that come to mind first when listing a category are the ones used as starting points for imagined aliens. Ease of retrieval beats typicality, familiarity or frequency in predicting use.
numbers: Exp 1: 30 people listed animals; 71 imagined alien animals. Imagination frequency correlated with output dominance r=.486 (150 animals), with dominance/rank .527; excluding 'human' r=.674 and .715. Rank correlated negatively (earlier listed, more used).
limits: Correlational item analysis. Students only. 'Human' item behaved as an outlier.
agent_relevance: Accessibility, not typicality, drives the start point. For a model: the first sample from a plain prompt is the most accessible item. Its frequency across many samples measures the default, and that can be counted by code.

source: Ward, Patterson, Sifonis, Dodds and Saunders (2002) The role of graded category structure in imaginative thought
finding: Nearly all imagined aliens carried the standard Earth-animal features, whether or not the person said they used a specific Earth animal. Those who said they relied on a specific animal produced less original creatures.
numbers: Sense organ 99%, appendage 97%, bilateral symmetry 91% (N=71). Originality: reliant on a specific Earth animal M=3.18 vs others M=4.34, t(69)=2.81, p<.01.
quote: Rather, it is a strategic approach, which happens to be dominant.
limits: Reliance self-reported after the task. Originality rated by judges.
agent_relevance: Structure is nearly universal, but the specific-exemplar route is optional. A scaffold can prefer a route (property-first, not exemplar-first) and test the originality gain.

source: Ward, Patterson, Sifonis, Dodds and Saunders (2002) The role of graded category structure in imaginative thought
finding: Exp 2 (tools for a creature with no appendages): people did not drop Earth tools; they adapted them. Handles became rare but mouthpieces and harnesses replaced them.
numbers: N=135. Handles 23% (constrained) vs 73% (control), chi-square(1)=33.20, p<.001. Mouthpieces 39% vs 1%, chi-square=29.03. Harnesses 20% vs 3%, chi-square=9.62, p<.01. Retrievability measures correlated with imagination frequency, dominance/rank r=.769 over 201 tools.
limits: Single constraint tested.
agent_relevance: A constraint makes the model modify the default, not abandon it. A hard constraint alone will not move the starting exemplar; the starting exemplar itself must be excluded.

source: Ward, Patterson, Sifonis, Dodds and Saunders (2002) The role of graded category structure in imaginative thought
finding: Exp 4 (imaginary fruit): an instruction to be creative changed little. An instruction not to feel bound by Earth fruit cut reliance on Earth fruit but left nearly half still relying on it.
numbers: N=203 in the generation task (36 in the listing task). Reliance on at least one Earth fruit: control 66%, 'be creative' 62% (n.s.), 'not bound' 48% (chi-square(1,N=153)=4.56, p<.05). Correlations of retrievability with imagination frequency significant in every condition (dominance/rank .70 to .93).
limits: Instruction effects are partial. Correlation pattern is stable, so ordering of what is used did not change.
agent_relevance: A plain 'be creative' line is nearly useless in people (4 points). A specific 'do not base it on X' line works somewhat (18 points). Matches the 'what to avoid' lead in the schema notes.

source: Birdsell (2019) Creative cognition: conceptual blending and expansion in a generative exemplar task
finding: Small classroom replication of the alien-creature task. Creatures again looked like Earth animals; a few drew idiosyncratic ones. Author looks at blending and expansion as the way out.
numbers: 34 students asked, 25 usable. Legs 72% of appendages; eyes 88% of sense organs; 75% had two eyes; just over half had a typical Earth-animal body; about 20% idiosyncratic.
limits: Small non-random class sample; a writing assignment, not a lab task. Descriptive only.
agent_relevance: Another instance that the effect is easy to reproduce. Low weight as evidence.

source: Agogue, Poirel, Pineau, Houde and Cassotti (2011) The impact of examples on creative design: explaining fixation and stimulation effects (ICED11)
finding: Fixation is a property of the default solution path. In the hen's egg drop task, most answers sit in one restrictive path. An example from that path lowers originality; examples that break the object's identity (expansive) raise it. Uses C-K theory to define restrictive vs expansive partitions.
numbers: Study 1: 81% of answers used an inert device (damp the shock 33%, protect 26%, slow the fall 22%); living device 4%, change egg properties 3%. Study 2: about 132 students, 10 min, five groups (control, parachute example, eagle example, freeze example, parachute plus eagle). Group effect on originality F(4,129)=11.219, p<.0005. Restrictive example less original than control (p<.005); expansive examples more original than control, p=.07 (not significant); restrictive plus expansive better than restrictive alone (p<.0005).
limits: Conference paper. Authors' stated sample 132 but df imply 134. Expansive effect only marginal. One task. Author list as recalled, not checked on the page.
agent_relevance: Gives a formula for our test: one 'expansive' example (changes what kind of thing the solution is) did not hurt and may help, while one common example hurts. Choose examples by distance from the default, never by quality.

source: Howard, Maier, Onarheim and Friis-Olivarius (2013) Overcoming design fixation through education and creativity methods (ICED13)
finding: Literature section only was read. Classifies fixation into three types (unconscious adherence, conscious blocking, intentional resistance; Youmans and Arciszewski 2012). Notes mixed results across a special issue: examples fixated in some studies, inspired in others. Cites Hernandez et al. (2010): examples improve novelty and variety, marginally worsen quantity and quality. Cites Howard et al.: stimuli shown after 30 min of brainstorming helped.
numbers: No new numbers read from this paper's own experiment.
quote: examples improve Novelty and Variety while it marginally worsens Quantity and Quality
limits: Secondary claims about other studies. The paper's own experiment was not read.
agent_relevance: Timing matters: examples after the first free burst helped, examples at the start fixated. Supports free-first, cue-later ordering in a loop.

source: Vasconcelos and Crilly (2016) Inspiration and fixation: questions, methods, findings, and challenges
finding: Review of 25 design studies that use the example-exposure method. Finds 14 manipulated variables and large variety in methods and results, so no single effect size is trustworthy. Describes Jansson and Smith (1991): designers shown an example repeated its features, some of them flawed, evidence of blind adherence; this persisted when told to avoid them.
numbers: 25 studies, 14 manipulated variables.
limits: Methodological review; no pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: Do not import a single design-fixation effect size. Measure fixation in our own set-up with a no-example arm.

source: Vasconcelos and Crilly (2016) Inspiration and fixation: questions, methods, findings, and challenges
finding: Evidence on instructions: Chrysikou and Weisberg (2005) found that merely telling people example features were bad was not enough; they had to be told to avoid them, and that made the task harder. Yilmaz et al. (2010) found no fixation with a do-not-repeat instruction. Jansson and Smith (1991), Perttula and Sipila (2007) and Smith et al. (1993) found copying despite instructions. The review calls the research equivocal.
limits: Mixed and not pooled. Differences in example type, task and scoring.
agent_relevance: 'Avoid X' works only when X is named and specific; vague 'be different' fails. Test named-feature avoid lists against vague ones in the LLM arm.

source: Vasconcelos and Crilly (2016) Inspiration and fixation: questions, methods, findings, and challenges
finding: Moderators reported: time away helps (Tsenn et al. 2014 more varied solutions after a long break; Youmans 2011 early interruption helps; Siangliulue 2015 interrupting with examples cut productivity). Abstract problem statements give divergence, concrete ones convergence (Zahner et al. 2010). Experienced designers made more novel solutions after an example than novices (Linsey et al. 2010). Industrial designers made more, more varied, more unique designs than mechanical engineers (Purcell and Gero 1996).
limits: Reported second-hand from the review. Not pooled.
agent_relevance: Candidate levers at equal compute: problem abstraction level, a pause with a changed cue, expert-style framing. Each can be run as an arm.

source: Fu, Sylcott and Das (2019) Using fMRI to deepen our understanding of design fixation
finding: Within-subject test, 10 design problems, 5 with an example solution and 5 without, in a scanner. Example exposure raised feature transfer but not novelty or quality. Brain activation shifted toward visuospatial areas and away from frontal areas near creative output.
numbers: Feature transfer 23% (example) vs 15% (no example), n=85 designs per condition, Friedman chi-square=3.6, p=.05. Quality: no significant difference. Novelty 0.71 vs 0.74, chi-square=3.12, p=.07. About 20 engineering students (some declined or excluded). Extra activation: right inferior temporal gyrus, left middle occipital, right superior parietal; less in left lingual and superior frontal gyri.
limits: p of .05 is borderline; small N; non-normal data; sketching in a scanner. Reverse inference from regions.
agent_relevance: Size of effect in a within-subject design is modest: 8 points of feature copying and no loss in rated quality or novelty. Expect small effects in our measurements too.

source: George and Wiley (2020) Need something different? Here's what's been done: effects of examples and task instructions on creative idea generation
finding: Alternate uses task (car tire). Exp 1: a verbal list of common example uses together with a warning to avoid them gave the most original ideas. Examples alone gave no gain. Exp 2: visual examples reduced originality (fixation); the avoid warning cut it but did not beat no examples.
numbers: Exp 1: 2x2, 36 per cell (N=144). Originality count: examples M=2.65 vs no examples 1.90, F(1,140)=4.85, p=.030; avoid M=2.68 vs no avoid 1.88, F(1,140)=5.60, p=.019. Examples+Avoid best vs rest: t(142)=3.51, p=.001, d=0.58 (count); ratio score d=0.51. Exp 2 figures not extracted.
limits: Student sample, one object, 3 min of ideas. Effects vary with how the examples are shown (verbal vs picture).
agent_relevance: Strongest direct support for 'show common ideas and say avoid them' as a cheap move (about half a standard deviation). Text vs image presentation changes the sign, so test the format.

source: Ricks, Turley-Ames and Wiley (2007) Effects of working memory capacity on mental set due to domain knowledge
finding: Replicates Wiley (1998): baseball experts do worse on Remote Associates items whose obvious baseball answer is wrong. More working memory helps generally, but not when a strong wrong candidate is active; it may then add focus on the wrong answer.
numbers: Exp 1: 58 analysed (after removing 3 of 61). Knowledge x problem type F(1,52)=5.58, p=.02, eta2=.10; three-way with WMC F(1,52)=3.30, p=.05, eta2=.11. Exp 2: 101 analysed (113 recruited). Authors warn Exp 1 participants may have guessed the study was about baseball.
limits: Small cells; one knowledge domain; possible demand effect in Exp 1.
agent_relevance: More capacity is not a cure for set. A larger model or longer chain may deepen the wrong frame. Compare small and large model fixation rates.

source: Chasing red herrings: memory of distractors causes fixation in creative problem solving (2018, Memory and Cognition)
finding: Fixation on Remote Associates Test items got worse when the wrong answers (red herrings) were practised in memory. Reinstating the context where the red herrings were learned made it worse again.
numbers: Exp 1 (N about 136): solved .44 (reinstated, no practice), .38 (reinstated, two retrievals), .42 (new, no practice); repetition F(1,132)=5.17, p=.025, partial eta2=.038; context main effect F<1. 15 s per item. Exp 2: primed with reinstated context 8% lower than unprimed (d=.43); primed with new context 3% lower (d=.16, n.s.).
limits: Effects small. Lab word puzzles. Context effect absent in Exp 1. Authors not read from the page text.
agent_relevance: Supports the retrieval-blocking account: strengthen the wrong answer in memory and fixation grows. For an agent, repeating a wrong attempt in context (retries) may reinforce it. Keep failed attempts out of the next prompt except as a short do-not list.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and intuition in creative problem solving
finding: Reports the meta-analysis of Sio and Ormerod (2009): 117 studies, a positive effect of delayed incubation, low to medium in size, larger when the break was filled by a demanding task or no task at all. The forgetting-of-fixation account needs time for set to decay.
numbers: Mean d=0.29 over 117 studies (as reported by Gilhooly).
limits: Second-hand figure; incubation is not defixation by technique. Author name taken from the OpenAlex title match, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: A break with a changed cue, at equal tokens, is a defixation option with a known small-to-medium size. For an LLM, forgetting means a context reset.

source: Cheng and Zhang (2025) Inspiration booster or creative fixation? The dual mechanisms of LLMs in shaping individual creativity in tasks of different complexity
finding: People brainstormed with a scripted LLM partner or a human partner. In a simple task (uses for a tire) the LLM partner lifted creativity; in a complex task (product feature design) it lowered creativity through measured fixation. Making the LLM answer in a constrained form with fewer ideas per reply reduced fixation in the complex task but weakened inspiration in the simple one.
numbers: Exp 1 N=204, Exp 2 N=204. Moderated mediation with 10,000 bootstrap draws: opposing indirect paths (inspiration vs fixation). Expert-coded creativity ICC=0.841 (Exp 2 fixation coding ICC=0.900).
limits: Fixation of humans on LLM ideas, not LLM self-fixation. Scripted idea pools. Exact effect sizes not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Angle B link. Fewer ideas per message cut fixation: an argument for showing one idea at a time between our own steps.

source: ScienceDaily / APS press release (2012) on McCaffrey, Innovation relies on the obscure: a key to overcoming the classic problem of functional fixedness
finding: Generic parts technique (GPT): break each object into parts, then ask (1) can it be broken down further? (2) does my description of the part imply a use? Re-describe the part generically (wick becomes a piece of string, then cotton strands). Trained people solved 8 functional fixedness problems more often. McCaffrey says all 1,001 historical inventions he analysed hinged on an obscure feature or function.
numbers: Reported: trained group solved the 8 problems 67% more often than untrained, and more than 8 times out of 10. Control rate, N and test statistics not given in this source.
quote: Does my description of the part imply a use?
limits: Press release only; the Psychological Science paper (23(3), 215-218) could not be opened. 67% is a relative figure. Independent replication not found in this session.
agent_relevance: A concrete operator: re-describe each component without use words, repeat once. Cheap to code as a restatement step; test against a plain retry at equal tokens.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider and Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Formal-style theory of why set breaks: people hold constraints (numbers cannot change, operators cannot change) and tight chunks. Insight needs the constraint relaxed or the chunk decomposed. Difficulty follows how broad the constraint is. Four matchstick-arithmetic experiments. The PDF was downloaded but is a scan with no text, so only a search summary was read.
numbers: Order of solution rate by problem type: A highest, then B, then C hardest (from search summary; percentages not read).
limits: Not read. Search summary only.
agent_relevance: Gives a computational handle on fixation: list the constraints the model assumes, then relax one at a time. Fits an operator that drops one named assumption.

source: Jansson and Smith (1991) Design fixation
finding: Founding design-fixation study. Student designers worked alone on a car-mounted bicycle rack, a measuring cup for the blind and a disposable spill-proof coffee cup. Those shown example pictures copied their features, including flawed ones, and kept doing so when told to avoid them. Described through the Vasconcelos and Crilly review and search summaries.
numbers: Exact counts not read.
limits: Paper not opened (paywalled). DOI as recalled, unchecked.
agent_relevance: The original 'told to avoid, still copied' result. Flawed examples being copied is the cleanest test of blind copying: plant a known flaw in the shot and check whether it propagates.

source: Duncker (1945) On problem-solving; Adamson (1952) Functional fixedness as related to problem solving
finding: Duncker showed people were slower and less likely to use the box as a platform when it held the tacks than when the tacks and box were separate. Adamson (1952) repeated it with adults. Read only through German and Defeyter and Glucksberg, which cite them.
numbers: Original figures not read; see Glucksberg 1962 values in line a01 (11.08 vs 3.67 min).
limits: Originals not opened. URL points to the citing paper.
agent_relevance: Founding paradigm. Test: preutilise an item in the prompt, then require its non-standard use.
